Case Report
A 60-year-old man complained of excessive daytime sleepiness
(Epworth sleepiness scale, 18/24) and nonrestorative sleep. His
spouse reported breathing pauses but no snoring.
A diagnosis of classic stiff person syndrome had been made
by corroborating his clinical presentation (stiffness in trunk
and in lumbar and abdominal muscles, hyperlordosis) with
electromyographic ﬁndings, which included continuous motor

activity and positive antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) (2,339 cpm; normal value , 180 cpm). His disease was
treated by intravenous immunoglobulin infusions. Comorbidities
included type 1 diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, Hashimoto thyroiditis,
and hypertension. His body mass index was 29 kg/m
2. There were
no signs of heart failure on physical examination.
Ventilatory polygraphy recorded respiratory events in a
periodic breathing pattern (Figure 1). Summary statistics
demonstrated an apnea –hypopnea index (AHI) of 83/h, a
predominance of central apneas (245 central apneas, 133
obstructive apneas, and 41 mixed apneas), and a mean oxygen
saturation as measured by pulse oximetry (Sp
O2) of 90%; he spent
42% of the sleep time with Sp O2 less than 90%. Lung function
testing was remarkable for a restrictive ventilatory de ﬁcit
(VC = 72% predicted; FEV 1 = 77% predicted; total pulmonary
capacity = 67% predicted). Measurement of blood gas tensions
showed a respiratory alkalosis and mild hypoxemia (pH = 7.48;
PaCO2 = 35 mm Hg; Pa O2 = 77 mm Hg).
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left
ventricular ejection fraction of 69%. The ventilatory response to
carbon dioxide measured by the rebreathing technique was elevated
(F
IO2 =9 5 % ; FICO2 = 5%; resting _VE = 14.2 L/min; end-tidal [partial]
carbon dioxide pressure [P ETCO2] = 33.5 mm Hg; _VE/PETCO2 =
7.5 L/min/mm Hg) (Figure 2). A brain magnetic resonance imaging
study showed no abnormality, particularly in the brainstem.
Adaptive servo-ventilation (AutoSetCS2; Resmed, St. Priest,
France) was introduced (pressure support, 3 –10 cm H
2O;
expiratory positive airway pressure, 5 cm H 2O) allowing
correction of AHI (to AHI = 4) and hypoxemia (mean Sp O2 = 94%;
time spent with Sp O2 , 90%, 0%). He quickly achieved optimal
adherence to the servo-ventilation device (7.5 h/night), and his
Epworth sleepiness scale scores were signi ﬁcantly improved
(ranging 1 –8 at his follow-up visits).
